points: WordPress is open source and has community support. Many hosting companies also offer plans that manage WordPress for you.
WordPress runs on PHP and stores content in MySQL or MariaDB.
You edit pages in your browser using the block editor.
You can change the layout with a theme and add features like contact forms with plugins.
The REST API lets another app pull posts from your site.
If you run the site yourself, you have to keep WordPress, your theme, and your plugins up to date.
If a developer stops maintaining a plugin you rely on, you may need to find a replacement.
Drupal is open source. The Drupal Association supports the project, and companies offer paid help with Drupal sites.
Drupal runs on PHP and can use databases such as MySQL or PostgreSQL.
Editors work in a browser. Drupal uses Twig templates to turn stored content into web pages.
You can set up different fields for different kinds of content. A school event could have a date and location, while a staff profile could have a job title and email.
One person can draft a page and another can approve it before it goes live.
Someone has to set up those fields, roles, and approval steps before staff can use them.
Before a major upgrade, you need to check whether your modules and theme support the new version.
The Ghost Foundation develops Ghost as open-source software. You can host it yourself or pay for Ghost(Pro).
Ghost runs on Node.js and uses MySQL 8 for production sites.
Writers use a browser editor. Handlebars templates control how posts look to readers.
You can publish an article on your site and send it to subscribers as a newsletter from the same editor.
You can make some posts free and reserve others for paying members.
Ghost uses Stripe for built-in subscription payments. If your publication uses another payment processor, connecting it takes extra work.
Torchbox created Wagtail. It is open source, with community contributors and commercial support available.
Wagtail uses Python and the Django framework. PostgreSQL is one database option.
Editors work in a browser, and Django templates control how the finished pages look.
A developer can give editors a set of blocks for text, photos, and quotes. Editors can then arrange those blocks as they build a page.
Editors can preview a draft and send it for approval.
Getting the site running takes coding experience. If editors need a new page type, a developer usually has to build it first.
Grav is open source. Its team and community maintain it, and the team also offers paid support.
Grav runs on PHP. It stores page content in Markdown files and settings in YAML files, so it can run without a database server.
Twig templates generate the pages. Editors can work in the browser using the admin panel.
You can install themes and plugins or set up pages in multiple languages.
Since the pages are files, you can track changes to the content in Git alongside changes to the code.
You need a host that runs PHP. I couldn't run Grav directly on GitHub Pages the way I host this class website.
If a project needs SQL queries to link records, Grav's page files don't provide that on their own.
